title: Is 'Agentic AI' a Fraud? What an Agent Actually Is, From Token Prediction to a Software Factory
short: Is Agentic AI a Fraud? What an Agent Actually Is
desc: A popular video calls agentic AI fraud. We test its 14 claims against the evidence: what an agent is, how often it works, and how to fence it from a plant.
keywords: agentic AI, AI agents, tool calling, function calling, agent loop, harness, MCP, SWE-bench, METR time horizon, compounding error, prompt injection, AI capex, OT security, IEC 62443, human in the loop, software factory
highlightClause: what an agent actually is, from token prediction to a software factory
subtitle: A widely shared video argues that agents are ordinary scripts wrapped in a next-token predictor and sold to rescue an industry that hit a wall. Each of its fourteen claims is graded here against the record: the mechanism, the measured reliability, the money, the name, and what an operations engineer should do when asked to put an agent on the BMS.

keyAnswer: In one breath: the critique is right about the mechanism and wrong about the absolutes. A language model does predict tokens, and an agent does act only through code someone wrote: the model proposes a structured call, a harness executes it and feeds the result back. But the model is not only a lookup of likely strings, the measured record of agents is real and improving, and the money is real too. What the record does show is that reliability compounds badly over many steps, so an agent is safe where deterministic checks decide which of its guesses reach the world, and never on a plant's control loop without an interlock.
